Build Your Own Centimeter-Accurate RTK N.summary: The Arduino Base & Next-Gen Rover Setup
body: If you’ve ever tried to build an autonomous rover, map a field, or track a drone, you know the frustration of standard GPS. Three to five meters of "accuracy" just doesn't cut it when you need precision. That’s where Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) positioning comes in.

Today, we're walking through an incredibly powerful, hybrid RTK hardware setup: using the tried-and-true ArduSimple simpleRTK2B (https://www.ardusimple.com/product/simplertk2b/) stacked as a top hat on an Arduino Uno Q (https://www.arduino.cc/product-uno-q/) for our Base Station, while deploying the brand-new, all-band simpleRTK4 Basic Starter Kit as our Rover.

By tying them together with NTRIP (Networked Transport of RTCM via Internet Protocol), you can cast your own correction data across the internet and get reliable, sub-centimeter accuracy anywhere with cell service. Let’s dive into the hardware!

To get centimeter-level accuracy, you need a fixed point of reference that knows exactly where it is. This base station observes the same satellites your rover sees, calculates the atmospheric and orbital errors, and sends those corrections out.

For our base, we are using the Arduino Uno Q, One of the easiest ways to handle serial data and pushing it to RTK2GO (http://rtk2go.com/) for casting. To turn this microcontroller into an RTK powerhouse, we are stacking the ArduSimple RTK2B directly on top of it as a shield (or "top hat").  The RTK2B is designed with Arduino headers. You simply click it into the Uno. No messy wiring, no breadboards and it can be powered by one USB C cable.
The RTK2B is powered by the u-blox ZED-F9P module, an absolute legend in the dual-band GNSS community. It supports L1 and L2 bands, making it highly reliable as a static base.

It is enclosed in a 3D printed case that I designed and built.  Something simple that exposes the SMA for the antenna and the usb-c connector to power the two boards.  To protect it from the element I covered it in a zip lock bag that is being held by a magnetic clip.  The antenna itself is being held onto the rail on my balcony with a 3D printed mount.
With our base station happily sitting on the balcony sending corrections to the cloud, it’s time to look at the Rover.

For this, we are using the RTK4.  While the base uses dual-band, the new simpleRTK4 features the u-blox ZED-X20P chip. This is an all-band receiver (L1, L2, L5, and L6).  Having access to L5 and L6 bands means the rover can lock into an RTK Fix (sub-centimeter accuracy) drastically faster than older modules, especially in challenging environments like under tree canopies or near tall buildings.

The kit from Ardusimple wasn’t really designed to be mounted on a rover rod.  I printed a mount to connect the rod 5/8 connector to the antenna.  There is a lot of cable with the u-blox ANN-MB-00 (https://www.ardusimple.com/product/ann-mb-00-ip67/) so I printed a cable wrap for it also.  For the module itself, I originally brought the case (https://www.ardusimple.com/product/plastic-case-simplertk2b/) for the board and still wanted to use it.  The last mount I created clips onto the case and has a drop in for my battery.

After several days of vibe coding in Claude Code, it finally gave me a working product.  It was able to write the code to receive the RTCM to the MCU that sends it to the MPU which pushes it to the RTK2GO server to cast.  The mount point is Fargo_ND.  I am using the in house GNSS Master (https://www.ardusimple.com/introducing-gnss-master-app/) to receive the correction data and push it to the rover.  A nice feature of the application is the receiver data output option, which allows a TCP Server mode.  Before I was using Android mock location, which removed all of the meta data from the receiver.  Applications such as QField and Mergin Maps allows for Network TCP or UDP input.
